0.note: The word translated as **chief musician** likely refers to the person in charge of music for worship. Some languages may have a term for a music leader. See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
See how you translated the expression “the sons of Korah” in the superscription to Psalm 42. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Korah] or [the Korahites]

The superscription to this wedding psalm uses the plural form **loves** to refer to the love of the king for his new wife and the love of the queen for her new husband. It may be more natural in your language to use the singular form. Alternate translation: [A love song]

1.note: The verb that the ULT translates as **boils over** occurs only here in the Bible, but it comes from the same root as a term for a pot or cauldron, so that seems to be its meaning. However, in this context, the focus is not on the heat that causes a liquid to boil. It is on the way a boiling liquid may overflow from a pot. Particularly if your language and culture associate heat with anger, it may be helpful to express the general meaning in order not to suggest that the psalmist is angry. Alternate translation: [My heart overflows with a good matter]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s thoughts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My mind overflows with a good matter] or [My thoughts about a good matter are overflowing]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **heart** (his mind) were actually overflowing with the **matter** he will describe in this psalm. He means that he finds his subject so inspiring that he cannot contain his thoughts about it; that is, he must speak out loud what he thinks about it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. (See the further discussion of this in the introduction to this psalm.) Alternate translation: [My subject is so inspiring that I must express my thoughts about it aloud]

The psalmist says **I am reciting** because he has already begun to sing his composition. However, since he is referring to the part of it that will follow, in some languages it may be more natural to use a verb in the future tense here. Alternate translation: [I will recite]

The psalmist is using the plural term **works** to refer to the many elements he has incorporated into this song. In some languages it may be more natural to use a singular term to refer to his entire composition. Alternate translation: [my work] or [my composition]

The phrase that the ULT translates as **to the king** may indicate: (1) that the psalmist is performing this song for the king and directing it to him. The ULT reflects this meaning. (2) that the psalmist has composed this song about the king. Alternate translation: [about the king]

The psalmist is speaking as if his **tongue** were actually a **stylus** that belonged to a **scribe** who was able to record quickly and accurately what he heard people say. The psalmist means that even though he has many thoughts that he would like to share on this occasion, he will be able to sing them all articulately and continuously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will be able to express all of my thoughts articulately and continuously in this song]

2.note: In verse 1, the psalmist was addressing all of his listeners. Here he begins to address the king directly. In some cultures, a person would not begin to speak to a ruler without using a specific form of address. If your culture has such a form, you could use it in your translation. Alternate translation: [Your Majesty, you are fairer than the sons of man]

2.q: יָפְיָפִ֡יתָ מִ⁠בְּנֵ֬י אָדָ֗ם ה֣וּצַק חֵ֭ן בְּ⁠שְׂפְתוֹתֶ֑י⁠ךָ
2.note: The words **You** and **your** are singular here and in the rest of the psalm because the psalmist is always addressing an individual. So use singular forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The psalmist is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” He is not implying that the king is not a man. He means that he is **fairer** or more handsome than all the other **sons of man**. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You are more handsome than other people]

The psalmist is making an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. (However, since an overstatement like this one was an appropriate compliment for a ruler in this culture, you may wish to retain the overstatement in your translation. The UST models one way to do that.) Alternate translation: [You are an exceptionally handsome man]

The psalmist is using or creating a special form of a verb that means “to be beautiful” by doubling its root. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [You are handsome, far more handsome than other men]

The expression **is poured** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. If you need to say who has done this action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [God has poured grace onto your lips]

The psalmist is speaking as if **Grace** had actually been **poured** onto the **lips** of the king. In context, the emphasis seems to be not on the action of pouring but on the result of pouring. When a liquid is poured onto a surface, it spreads out and covers that surface. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Grace covers your lips] or [Your lips are entirely gracious]

Here the king’s **lips** represent his speech. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your speech is entirely gracious]

The psalmist is not using the word **Therefore** to indicate that the king’s attractive appearance and gracious speech are the reasons why **God** has **blessed** him. He means that these characteristics of the king are evidence that God has blessed him. If a term such as “therefore” would not communicate this meaning in your language, you may want to use a different connecting word or phrase to show how the following statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [This is how we know that]

3.note: The psalmist is using one action that a **warrior** would do in preparation for fighting a battle, strapping his **sword** onto his **thigh**, to refer to being equipped for battle in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Prepare yourself to do battle]

While the expression **Gird** is an imperative, the psalmist is not telling the king to do something or suggesting that he is not already doing it. Instead, the psalmist is celebrating what the king is already doing. It may be more natural in your language to express this meaning by using a form other than an imperative. Alternate translation: [You are always prepared to do battle]

As the next verse indicates, the psalmist wants the king to use his power specifically to uphold justice. This may not necessarily involve fighting an actual battle. You could indicate this in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Be prepared to use your power to uphold justice] or [You are always prepared to use your power to uphold justice]

Together the terms **glory** and **majesty** express a single idea. The word **majesty** characterizes this man as a king, and the word **glory** tells what kind of king he is, specifically when he fights for justice. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [as a glorious king]

4.note: See how you represented the term “majesty” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [And as a king]

The phrase **prosper, ride out** expresses a single idea. The word **prosper**, meaning “succeed” or “triumph,” tells in what way the psalmist wants the king to **ride out** in his chariot. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [ride out triumphantly] or [ride out to victory]

The psalmist is speaking as if he actually wanted the king to **ride out** in his chariot to fight a battle. As in the previous verse, he wants the king to use his power to uphold justice without necessarily involve fighting an actual battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [use your power triumphantly]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **truth**, **humility**, and **righteousness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to establish a reign that is truthful, humble, and righteous]

The psalmist is speaking of the king’s **right hand** as if it were a living thing that could **teach** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May you discover that you can do fearful things with your right hand]

The psalmist is using the king’s **right hand** to represent him using his sword and shooting arrows with that hand or, more generally, to represent him fighting against his enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May you discover that you can do fearful things by using your sword and shooting arrows] or [May you discover that you can do fearful things as you fight against your enemies]

The expression **fearful things** is a passive verbal form, a participle that the psalmist is using as a noun. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [things that terrify your opponents]

5.q: חִצֶּ֗י⁠ךָ שְׁנ֫וּנִ֥ים עַ֭מִּים תַּחְתֶּ֣י⁠ךָ יִפְּל֑וּ בְּ֝⁠לֵ֗ב אוֹיְבֵ֥י הַ⁠מֶּֽלֶךְ
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that the arrows are **in the heart of the enemies of the king** with the information that the **arrows are sharp**. Alternate translation: [Your arrows are sharp in the heart of the enemies of the king; the peoples fall under you]

The psalmist says that these **arrows** are **sharp** to mean that they penetrate through armor into the bodies of enemy soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your arrows penetrate]

The psalmist is speaking as if **the peoples** who fight against the king actually **fall** down dead or wounded and he drives his chariot over them, so that they are **under** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you win victory over the peoples]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. If you decide not to move this phrase to an earlier part of the verse, after **Your arrows are sharp**, you can supply those words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Your arrows are in the heart of the enemies of the king] or [Your arrows penetrate into the heart of the enemies of the king]

In this verse, the word **heart** is singular in form, but it refers to the hearts of all of the king’s **enemies**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “heart.” Alternate translation: [in the hearts of]

The psalmist is speaking of the king in the third person even though he is addressing him directly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [your enemies] or [your enemies, O king]

6.note: Here the king’s **throne** represents his reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Your reign]

The Hebrew term that is translated as “God” in most contexts can sometimes be used to refer respectfully to judges. There are probable examples of this in Exodus 21:6, Exodus 22:9, Exodus 22:28, and Psalm 82:1. Since the rest of this verse speaks of the king enforcing justice, this seems to be another instance of that usage. (The psalmist clarifies in the next verse that the king is subject to God himself, who is his God.) To avoid the impression that the psalmist is addressing the king as if he were God or a god, it may be helpful to use a comparable respectful form of address in your language. (See the further discussion of this in the introduction to this psalm.) Alternate translation: [O royal judge]

Here the king’s **scepter** represents his rule. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [You rule your kingdom with justice]

7.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **righteousness** and **wickedness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [You love right actions, and you hate wicked actions]

The psalmist is speaking as if **God** had actually **anointed** the king with **oil** that consisted of or imparted **joy**. The image of pouring out a fluid so that it covers someone conveys the idea of abundance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [has given you abundant joy, more than your companions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [has made you very joyful, more than your companions]

8.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the king’s **garments** were actually made of the spices **Myrrh**, **aloes**, and **cassia**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all of your garments are fragrant with myrrh and aloes and cassia] or [myrrh, aloes, and cassia scent all of your garments]

**Myrrh**, **aloes**, and **cassia** are fragrant spices. If your readers would not be familiar with these spices, we do not recommend that you use the names of similar spices that your readers might recognize, since the psalmist is describing a real historical situation. Instead, you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [Fragrant spices]

The psalmist is using the plural **palaces** where he could have used the singular form. This suggests that he is using the plural form to emphasize the vast extent of the king’s palace complex, which may include several buildings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the singular and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [your vast palace of]

The psalmist is using **stringed instruments** to represent the music that people are playing on those instruments. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the music of stringed instruments is making you rejoice]

9.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **precious** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. (The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**.) Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [are among your honored women] or [are among the ladies of your court]

The expression **is stationed** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [is standing]

Having the **queen** stand at his **right hand** (that is, on his right side) was a symbolic action by which the king honored his bride. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [in a place of honor at your right side]

Here, **gold of Ophir** represents garments decorated with that very fine gold, as verses 13 and 14 indicate. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in garments decorated with gold of Ophir]
The word **Ophir** is the name of a land that produced gold of excellent quality.

10.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and do that here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully, daughter, and consider] or [Listen, daughter, and consider, yes, incline your ear]

The psalmist is addressing the bride with the courteous and gentle expression that wise older people in this culture used to address young people whom they were teaching. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [young lady]

The psalmist is speaking as if he wants the bride physically to **incline** her **ear**, that is, to lean over the way someone would do to pay close attention to someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and pay close attention]

The psalmist is speaking as if he wanted the bride actually to **forget** her nation and family. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not wish that you were still with your people and in the house of your father]

Here the term **house** represents the “household” of the bride’s **father**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and your family]

11.note: The psalmist is using one part of the bride, her **beauty**, to mean all of her in the act of being attractive to the king. The psalmist means that if she gives the king her exclusive devotion, as he advised her in the previous verse, not just her physical appearance but her qualities of loyalty and faithfulness will make the king appreciate and love her. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [This will make you very attractive to the king]

Bowing low to the ground in front of the king was a symbolic action by which the bride showed her acceptance of his authority over her both as her new husband and as her new king. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [prostrate yourself respectfully and submissively to him]

12.q: וּ⁠בַֽת־צֹ֨ר ׀ בְּ֭⁠מִנְחָה פָּנַ֥יִ⁠ךְ יְחַלּ֗וּ עֲשִׁ֣ירֵי עָֽם
12.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from later in the verse if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [The rich of the people will entreat your face; the daughter of Tyre will do so with a gift]

The psalmist is speaking as if the city of **Tyre** were a mother and its people were its **daughter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The people of Tyre]

The psalmist may be using one particularly wealthy and influential kingdom, **Tyre**, to represent foreign kingdoms in general. This would be complementary to **the people** of Israel or Judah whom he mentions later in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Representatives of foreign kingdoms]

The psalmist is using the adjective **rich** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the rich citizens among our people]
Here the queen’s **face** represents her “favor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your favor]

13.q: כָּל־כְּבוּדָּ֣ה בַת־מֶ֣לֶךְ פְּנִ֑ימָה מִֽ⁠מִּשְׁבְּצ֖וֹת זָהָ֣ב לְבוּשָֽׁ⁠הּ
13.note: In this poem celebrating the king’s wedding, the psalmist is not following a strict chronological sequence. In verse 9, he presented a portrait of the bride, groom, and attendants in their formal places at the ceremony. In verses 13–15, he describes the procession of the bride and her attendants to the ceremony. That procession took place before he started singing this song, so in some languages, it may be appropriate to describe them in a past tense. The UST models one way to do that.

By **the daughter of the king**, the psalmist means the same person whom he calls the “queen” in verse 9. (This indicates that her father is the **king** of a foreign country.) You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the royal bride]
The psalmist is using the term **within** to mean a room or apartment within the palace where the bride has dressed for her wedding. Alternate translation: [in her chamber]

14.note: The expression **will be led** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Royal officials will lead her]

The psalmist is addressing the king once again, as the pronoun **you** at the end of the verse indicates. So it may be more natural in some languages to use a second-person form here. Alternate translation: [to you, O king,]

Here, **embroidery** represents embroidered garments, that is, garments decorated with embroidery. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in embroidered garments]

The term **embroidery** describes the art of making decorative designs in cloth by using needles to work colored threads into it to make beautiful images or patterns. If your readers would not be familiar with what embroidery is, in your translation you could use a general expression. Alternate translation: [in garments decorated with colored thread]

The expression **will be brought** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Royal officials will bring her companions to you, the virgins who follow her]

15.note: The psalmist is speaking of **joy** and **rejoicing** as if they were living things that could lead the bride and her attendants into the king’s palace. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [There will be joy and rejoicing as they will enter]

The terms **joy** and **rejoicing** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [with great joy]
See how you translated the similar expression “to the king” in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [into your palace, O king]

16.note: The psalmist is using the term **fathers** to represent “ancestors,” and he is using the term **sons** to represent “descendants.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestors … your descendants]
Since the psalmist is referring to multiple people (**sons** or descendants), it may be more natural in many languages to use a plural pronoun here. Alternate translation: [you will make them]

The psalmist is saying **all** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. (However, since an overstatement like this one was an appropriate compliment for a ruler in this culture, you may wish to retain the overstatement in your translation, as the UST does. See what you decided to do in verse 2.) Alternate translation: [in many parts of the world]

17.note: Here the king’s **name** represents his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [in every generation] or [from generation to generation]
